subtype: Approach: assigns jobs by each person's strengths [Thinking]
passage: Sahil, you are captain this year, so hear how Deepak did it at fifteen. Our school was planning Sports Day and I had a list as long as my arm and no idea who should do what. I would have painted the posters myself, badly. Then I thought: who in my class writes like a printed book? Nusrat. And who knows every shopkeeper on the road and could get the permission letters signed at the ward office? Gopal. I did not pick names out of a hat. I went to Nusrat and said, "Your writing is the best in our class, will you do the posters?" Then to Gopal: "You know people, can you get the permissions?" Both said yes at once, because I had named what they were good at. I kept the sports list for myself.

qa.q: Who was asked to do the posters?
qa.a: Nusrat was asked to do the posters.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel at the start, holding a list as long as an arm?
qa.a: Deepak felt overwhelmed and unsure who should do what.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made both classmates say yes, and why?
qa.a: Deepak named what each classmate was good at, so the request felt like a recognition of a real skill.

qa.q: How might Gopal have felt when asked about the permissions?
qa.a: Gopal may have felt pleased and trusted, since the request showed that Deepak had noticed the skill.

grounding: Shows a student captain choosing a poster maker and a permissions person by what each is good at.

subtype: Approach: hands over a task with clear expectations and a check-in time [Action]
passage:
In the computer lab, Reena pulled a chair up beside Vidya. "I need the survey data cleaned. Can you take that on?"

"Sure. Cleaned how?"

"One row per student, dates as day-month-year, blank answers marked NA, not left empty. Here's a finished example of two rows." Reena slid a printout across. "What matters is that I can load it straight into the chart tool."

Vidya wrote the format in her notebook and read it back. "Should I message you if something looks odd?"

"Please. And send me the first fifty rows on Wednesday morning, so I can check the format before you do the rest."

"Wednesday, first fifty. Got it."

On Wednesday at ten the sample arrived. Reena found one date column in the wrong order, told Vidya, and Vidya fixed it before starting on the remaining rows.

qa.q: By when did Reena ask for a sample?
qa.a: Reena asked for the first fifty rows on Wednesday morning.

qa.q: What did Vidya seem to want when asking whether to message if something looked odd?
qa.a: Vidya wanted to be sure what to do if unsure, which shows care about avoiding mistakes and feeling trusted with the task.

qa.q: What could Reena do if the sample still has problems on Wednesday?
qa.a: Reena could point to the exact rows and the rule that was missed and agree a second short check, rather than taking the work over.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel about the Wednesday check?
qa.a: Vidya might feel supported, since the problem was caught early instead of being judged after all the work was done.

grounding: Shows a student lead handing over data cleaning with a clear format and a check-in time.

subtype: Approach: hands off work but keeps redoing it because it is not done her way [Pitfall]
passage:
Vasudha had been made team lead at the cooperative office in the small town only a month before. On Monday she handed the monthly collections report to Yamini. "Do it the way you think best."

On Thursday Yamini brought it: tidy tables and a short summary. Vasudha read two pages, frowned and said, "I'll just fix a few things." By night she had rewritten every table in her own layout and swapped out the summary. On Friday morning Yamini opened the file and saw none of her own words. She said nothing, put her pen down and went to check the ledger, quieter than usual.

The next month, when Vasudha asked who could take the report, the room went still. She stayed until eight, doing all of it herself.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do after reading two pages of the report?
qa.a: Vasudha said she would just fix a few things, and then rewrote every table.

qa.q: How might Yamini have felt on seeing none of her own words in the file?
qa.a: Yamini probably felt distrusted and discouraged, shown by saying nothing and going quiet.

qa.q: What could Vasudha do instead of rewriting the whole report?
qa.a: Vasudha could say clearly what the report needs before it starts, then comment on one or two specific points and let Yamini make the changes.

qa.q: Why might the team go quiet when Vasudha asks who can take the report?
qa.a: They may fear that their work will simply be redone, so nobody wants to put in the effort.

grounding: Shows a new lead delegating a report and rewriting it entirely, leaving the colleague distrusted and doubling her own work.

subtype: Approach: agrees what good looks like, then steps back and gives feedback [Revision]
passage:
Monday. Anirban used to send colleagues step-by-step instructions. This time he told Sahil only the outcome. "I need a one-page guide that a new customer can follow in five minutes. How you build it is up to you." Sahil nodded slowly, surprised.

Wednesday. Anirban's fingers hovered over the chat window, ready to ask about progress. Instead he waited. Across the office, Sahil was drawing a flowchart with four boxes.

Friday. Sahil sent the guide. Anirban gave it to a tester from sales, who followed it in four minutes. "It works. One thing: the second box says onboarding. Can it say first login?" Sahil changed it in ten minutes. "Thanks for not telling me how," Sahil said.

qa.q: How long should a new customer need to follow the guide?
qa.a: A new customer should be able to follow it in five minutes.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when Anirban gave only the outcome?
qa.a: Sahil felt surprised, and perhaps pleased to be trusted with the method.

qa.q: What could Anirban do if the guide had failed the test?
qa.a: Anirban could explain exactly where the tester got stuck and ask Sahil to revise it, keeping the choice of method with Sahil.

qa.q: How might the tester from sales see the guide?
qa.a: The tester would find it clear, since it took only four minutes to follow, and would be glad the test helped improve it.

grounding: Shows a lead stating the outcome needed, letting the colleague choose the method and giving feedback on the result.

subtype: Approach: brings a problem to a caregiver [Action]
passage:
Mili sat on the floor with a plastic pot, pulling at its lid. It would not open. She grunted, pushed, and then gave a small whimper. She crawled to Mummy and held the pot up high.

"What have you got, Mili?"

"Ah! Ah!"

"Stuck? Let Mummy see." Mummy twisted the lid slowly, so Mili could watch the turn. "Pop!"

Mili patted the pot, then pushed it back into Mummy's hands. "Again!"

"Again? All right, close it."

qa.q: What did Mili hold up to Mummy?
qa.a: Mili held up the plastic pot.

qa.q: What did Mili want when she whimpered?
qa.a: Mili wanted the lid opened and needed help, since she could not manage it alone.

qa.q: What could Mummy do to help Mili learn?
qa.a: Mummy could twist the lid slowly and let Mili put her hands on it too.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel when Mili brought the pot over?
qa.a: Mummy might feel pleased that Mili came to ask for help instead of giving up.

grounding: Shows a toddler bringing a toy with a stuck lid to her mother and whimpering for help.

subtype: Approach: asks a trusted adult a direct question [Action]
passage:
Ojas sat on the shop step in the small town with one school shoe on and the other's laces hanging loose. He tried, twisted, and the laces slid apart. He sighed. "Dada, will you show me how to tie it?"

Dada put down the newspaper. "Watch slowly, beta. Cross. Tuck. Make a bunny ear."

Ojas watched, chin on his knees. Then Dada put his big hands over Ojas's small ones, and together they pulled the loops tight. "Now you."

Ojas stuck out his tongue and crossed the laces alone. The bow was lopsided, but it held. "I did it!"

qa.q: What did Dada say to do?
qa.a: Dada said to cross, tuck and make a bunny ear.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel after tying the bow?
qa.a: Ojas felt proud and happy, and called out "I did it!"

qa.q: What could Ojas do to get better at tying the bow?
qa.a: Ojas could practise a little each day with Dada nearby, and ask to be shown slowly again if he gets stuck.

qa.q: How might Dada feel while showing Ojas?
qa.a: Dada might feel patient and pleased to see Ojas learn.

grounding: Shows a child asking his grandfather to show him how to tie laces and trying with the grandfather's hands guiding his.

subtype: Approach: seeks a teacher when stuck after trying alone [Thinking]
passage:
Abhinav here. I sit behind Manjula, so I saw everything. The problem said a rope is 12 metres long and is cut into pieces of 3 metres. How many pieces? Manjula worked on it for ten minutes, biting her pencil. Then she picked up her notebook and walked to the teacher's desk.

"I tried, Ma'am. I did 12 minus 3 and got 9. But 9 doesn't sound like pieces."

The teacher looked at her page. "What does 9 tell you?"

"It's the rope left after one cut. I have to keep cutting... oh! It's 12 shared into 3s." She wrote 4 and smiled. I don't know if she felt silly or happy, but she ran back to her seat fast.

qa.q: What answer did Manjula get when she did 12 minus 3?
qa.a: Manjula got 9.

qa.q: How was Manjula feeling about her answer of 9, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Manjula felt doubtful and unsure, since she said 9 did not sound like pieces, so she wanted help finding the mistake.

qa.q: What could Manjula try next time she is stuck?
qa.a: Manjula could draw the rope cut into pieces first, and bring her attempt to the teacher if she is still stuck.

qa.q: Why can Abhinav only guess how Manjula felt at the end?
qa.a: Abhinav sat behind and saw only the smile and the quick run back, so cannot know Manjula's feelings for sure.

grounding: Shows a girl trying a maths problem alone and then showing the teacher her attempt so the mistake in her thinking can be seen.

subtype: Approach: prepares questions before meeting a professional [Action]
passage:
Subject: Thank you for Tuesday

Dear Pallavi,

Thank you for meeting me at the coffee counter. I came with three questions written on a card, and your answers were clear. First, skills: you said to get comfortable with spreadsheets and with writing short, clear updates. Second, entry paths: an internship in third year, or a junior analyst opening through campus placements. Third, daily work: mostly cleaning data in the mornings and meetings after lunch. I took notes on all of it, and next week I will compare them with what a second alumnus tells me. I have already signed up for a spreadsheet course. Thank you again for your time.

Best wishes,
Lokesh

qa.q: What were the three questions about?
qa.a: The three questions were about skills, entry paths and daily work.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt going into the meeting with a card of written questions?
qa.a: Lokesh probably felt keen but a little nervous, wanting to make good use of the time and get a clear picture for planning.

qa.q: What could Lokesh do with the notes next?
qa.a: Lokesh could compare them with the second alumnus's answers, see what matches, and choose a first step.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt on receiving a student with prepared questions?
qa.a: Pallavi may have felt pleased and respected, since the student took time to prepare.

grounding: Shows a student visiting an alumnus with three written questions and taking notes to compare later.

subtype: Approach: treats an expert's view as final without asking the reasons [Pitfall]
passage: Darshan here. I run the stall next to Anusha's at the weekend market, so I heard the whole thing. Farhan, an adviser from the city, told Anusha, "Double your price on the handmade candles. Premium sells." Anusha wrote it down and nodded at every line. I did not hear a single "why". The next Saturday, candles that sold at forty went up to eighty. Nobody bought. Farhan's customers in the city pay for the box and the fancy label; ours are neighbours who compare with the shop by the bus stand. By afternoon Anusha's table was still full and she was rearranging it for the third time. I don't know if Anusha blamed the advice or the customers. She only said, "He's the expert."

qa.q: What did Farhan tell Anusha to do?
qa.a: Farhan told Anusha to double the price on the handmade candles.

qa.q: How might Anusha have felt as the candles did not sell?
qa.a: Anusha probably felt worried and uncertain, but covered it by saying "He's the expert."

qa.q: What could Anusha have asked Farhan before changing the price?
qa.a: Anusha could have asked why he suggested it and whether it works in a small weekend market like hers, or tried the new price on only some candles.

qa.q: How might customers at the market see the doubled price?
qa.a: Customers might compare it with the shop by the bus stand and think it too much for a market stall.

grounding: Shows an entrepreneur following an adviser's pricing tip without asking why, missing that the adviser's market differs from hers.

subtype: Approach: asks for the reasoning and checks it against a second source [Revision]
passage: I'm Irawati, and last spring I asked a question I used to be too shy to ask. My adviser said, "Offer free delivery, always." The old me would have printed it on flyers that night. This time I asked, "Why?" She explained that in the big city people will not order without it, and the cost gets spread over many orders. That made sense for her city, but my town has one main road. So I asked Jahnavi, who runs a bakery in a town like mine. Jahnavi laughed. "Free delivery ate half my first month." I settled on free delivery only for the two nearest lanes, and a small charge beyond. Three months on, orders are steady and the numbers still make sense.

qa.q: What did Irawati ask the adviser?
qa.a: Irawati asked the adviser, "Why?"

qa.q: What was Irawati thinking when she heard the adviser's reasons?
qa.a: Irawati realised the reasoning fitted the adviser's city but not a town with one main road, so she felt doubtful about using it as it was.

qa.q: What could Irawati do to check her final delivery rule?
qa.a: Irawati could track orders and delivery costs for a few weeks and change the lanes or the charge if the numbers do not fit.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have felt when sharing that experience?
qa.a: Jahnavi may have felt glad to help and open about a costly lesson, since Jahnavi laughed and gave a plain answer.

grounding: Shows a person asking an adviser why, checking with another practitioner, and adapting the advice to her own customers.
